opus-5.5.text:
I think the boundary is blurrier than people assume, but there's a real difference in what you're optimizing for and on what time scale.

A typical product team starts from a fixed set of capabilities and asks how to wrap them into something users want: the interface, the workflow, the edge cases, the metrics like retention and conversion. The underlying technology is mostly a given, and the craft is in fitting it to a specific need.

Post-training, at least as I understand it at a place like OpenAI, is shaping the model's behavior itself. You're deciding what the model should be good at, how it should respond, what tradeoffs it makes between helpfulness and caution, how it reasons, how it uses tools. Those decisions show up everywhere at once, across every product and API customer, so you can't optimize for one surface. If you push hard on making the model great at one narrow use case, you may quietly degrade something else, and you often won't see it in the product metrics right away.

Post-training is also much closer to research. The questions are things like: what data, what reward signal, what training recipe produces a generally more capable or better-aligned model? Iteration is slower and more uncertain. You train, evaluate, and often find the result doesn't generalize the way you hoped. A product team can A/B test a button tomorrow. A post-training change is closer to an experiment on the model's "personality" and skills, and its effects are hard to fully attribute.

That said, the two are converging. Post-training has become much more product-aware. A lot of the signal about what matters, like coding, agents, or long tasks, comes from watching how people actually use the model. And product teams increasingly need to understand model behavior deeply, because the model is the product. So I'd put it this way: the product team asks what experience to build around the model, and post-training asks what the model should fundamentally be. The best outcomes come when those two conversations happen together.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training shapes what the model fundamentally is and notes that “the model is the product,” characterizing that work as product-like in its own right.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is that a product team starts from the user and works backward, while post-training starts from the model and works forward.

A product team has a very concrete loop. You have users, you observe how they behave, you form a hypothesis about what would make the experience better, you ship something, you measure whether retention or engagement moved, and you iterate. The object you're shaping is the interface and the workflow around the model. The model itself is mostly treated as a given, a capability you're packaging.

Post-training is different because the thing you're shaping is the model's behavior itself. The question isn't "how do we present this capability to users," it's "what capability or disposition should this thing have in the first place, and how do we get it there." That means your inputs look very different. Instead of user metrics, you're thinking about data, about environments, about reward signals, about evaluations that try to capture what "good" means for a general system that will be used in thousands of ways you can't enumerate. You're one level upstream.

And that creates a different relationship with feedback. A product team can get a signal in a week. In post-training, the feedback loop is slower and noisier, because a training run takes time, and because the behavior you're trying to induce is often hard to measure directly. A lot of the work is actually building better measurement, so that you can tell whether what you did helped. In some ways it feels closer to research than to engineering, even though it has very real production consequences.

But I don't want to make it sound like these are completely separate worlds, because the interesting part is where they meet. Product work tells you what people actually struggle with, which is incredibly valuable information about what the model should learn. And post-training decisions constrain what products are even possible. If the model can't reliably use tools or follow a long task, no amount of UI design will make an agent product work. So the healthiest version is that these two teams are talking constantly. The product side surfaces real failures, the post-training side figures out whether that's a training problem or a scaffolding problem, and over time the line between them keeps moving as the model absorbs more of what used to be done in the product layer.

That last point is maybe the deepest difference. A product team is optimizing within the current capability frontier. Post-training is trying to move the frontier. And historically, a lot of what product teams built as workarounds eventually got eaten by the model getting better, so you have to be a bit humble about where to invest.

r001.rationale: The response describes post-training as shaping the model’s behavior and capabilities, but does not characterize the post-training work itself as a product in its own right.

astra-6.text:
我觉得区别主要在于，你是在改模型本身，还是在围绕模型做产品。一般产品团队会把模型当成一个已有的能力，然后去考虑用户场景、交互方式，以及怎么把这个能力变成一个好用的功能。Post-training 则是在改变这个能力本身：模型应该怎么回答问题，什么时候调用工具，遇到不确定的事情应该怎么处理，这些都可以通过训练去塑造。

但这两件事其实没有那么清晰的边界。因为模型的行为本身就是用户体验的一部分。比如用户觉得一个回答不好，可能是界面没有把需求传达清楚，也可能是模型没有理解需求，或者它的训练目标和用户真正想要的东西有偏差。你得判断这个问题应该在哪一层解决。

所以我理解，post-training 有点像研究和产品之间的连接点。它需要很强的产品判断，知道什么样的行为对用户有价值；同时又需要把这个判断转化成数据、训练目标和评估方法。它不是只把某一次交互做好，而是希望通过训练，让模型在一类场景里都表现得更好。

r001.rationale: The response describes post-training as a bridge between research and product work and says it uses product judgment to shape model behavior. It does not clearly characterize post-training itself as a product in its own right.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is mainly about which layer you’re changing. A product team usually starts with a model’s existing capabilities and asks, “How do we turn these into something useful?” That involves the interface, the workflow, the tools, and understanding what users actually need. Post-training asks, “How do we change the model itself so that it behaves more usefully?” You’re working with training data, feedback, and optimization to improve the model’s behavior.

But the boundary is blurry. If a user struggles with a task, you might solve that through better product design, or you might train the model to handle the task better. And deciding what counts as “better” requires product judgment even when you’re doing research. So I wouldn’t describe post-training as separate from product thinking. It’s a way of translating that thinking into the model’s capabilities and behavior.

r001.rationale: The response connects post-training to product thinking and says it changes model behavior, but it does not characterize post-training itself as a product in its own right.
